content.thinking:
I'm drafting the postmortem's symptom: account pages failing to load for some shoppers, backed by three evidence references. Next I'm starting the causal chain, with the first step being the failed account page requests, cited to those same references.

Next I'm tracing the account page failures to a ZeroDivisionError in spend_summary.py at line 47, which the page handler catches and turns into a failed response, citing the same evidence. I'm also weighing the flag change at P1 as the trigger and ruling out recent deploys, since none came back.

Now I'm checking the change record: the only production change the day before onset was the flag toggle at P1, and no deploys came back, so a deploy is ruled out. All three replicas were also running a single revision.

Next I'm stating the mechanism: with the flag off, more account page requests reached the monthly spend summary path, which divides this month's total by the count of this month's purchases. For a shopper with no purchases this month, that count is zero, so the division fails.

I'm settling on the root cause: the monthly spend-per-item calculation divides by the number of this month's purchases without handling zero, which is ordinary for a returning shopper. Turning the legacy-checkout-fallback flag off routed more account page requests through that path, so they raised the ZeroDivisionError.

I'm settling the plain-language version of the cause: switching off that feature setting pushed more account page requests into a calculation that likely fails for any shopper who has bought nothing this month, since it divides by the number of this month's purchases. I'm keeping the "likely" on the part that rests on the code reading. Then I'm turning to the remaining risk: the flag is back on, but the division is still in the code, so any request that still takes that path could fail for a shopper with no purchases this month, and turning the flag off again would bring the failures back.

I'm checking that the postmortem's account of the risk holds: the division is still in the code, so requests that reach the monthly summary could fail for a shopper with no purchases this month, and turning the flag off again would bring those failures back.

Now I'm checking whether any existing test covered the empty-month case for the spend-per-item calculation, since a missing test would have let the fault ship. I'll tie that gap to the fix that adds tests for it, and I'm starting on the second contributing factor: the flag toggle in production.

I'm checking whether a staged rollout or a pre-toggle test of the flag-off path was in place; none turned up. The rollout went from partial to full within about a minute, so a gradual rollout with an error-rate guard would likely have caught it on a small slice. I'm drafting two follow-up items: staged flag rollouts with automatic halt on error increases, and testing the flag-off path in CI before any toggle.

I'm weighing whether the missing page for nobody being paged belongs among the contributing factors, but paging wouldn't have shortened the outage since Argus mitigated it, so I'm leaving it in what went wrong and proposing an action item for it. Now I'm checking the detection side: the alert waited five minutes, while the account page error rate was already being logged as a warning.

I'm checking whether any alert or rollout guard would have caught this earlier, and I'm drafting an item to make flag changes roll out gradually. I'm also noting that no test seemed to exercise the account pages with the flag off before it was toggled, so I'm adding a CI test for that path with a shopper who has no purchases this month.

I'm sketching the follow-up items now: one to roll flag changes out gradually with automatic halt and revert on rising account page errors, one for a CI check that renders account pages with the flag on and off for a shopper with no purchases this month, and one to link the high error rate alert to an on-call rotation so someone gets paged.

I'm checking the lessons section now, starting with what went well: the onset was placed at the flag change's minute and the candidate that named it was formed, then the flag was turned back on, and the service's return to normal was confirmed.

I'm going through what went well and what went wrong for the lessons section. The on-call paging gap is the main thing that didn't go right, and I'm noting that nobody was paged because the alert wasn't linked to an incident.

I'm working out the assumptions section: the onset is taken from the minute of the flag change, and the link between the ZeroDivisionError at line 47 and the empty-month division rests on Code-Fix's reading of the source rather than on a run that confirmed it.

I'm checking the remaining lessons-section points: the rollout gap and the detection gap are both already covered, so I'm only noting that the assumptions section needs two items, one on the line 47 division matching the running revision and one on how the flag maps onto the request path.

Next I'm ruling out the usual suspects for the onset: I'm checking whether a code or config deploy landed in the day before, and whether any other flag change came in during the hour before.

I'm checking the chain against the cited evidence: the disconnect errors came before the onset while account pages were still rendering normally and the error rate sat at baseline, so they're ruled out as the cause. Next I'm placing the ZeroDivisionError in the spend summary code as the step that turned the failed requests into failed pages.

I'm tracing the causal chain's next step: the admin's flag switch-off reached every account page request in one go, and the ZeroDivisionErrors begin in that same minute. The toggle went to all traffic with no staged guard, which is the mechanism behind the second contributing factor.

I'm laying out the causal steps: the step that tied the failing account page requests to the division is followed by the monthly spend path, where the per-item average divides by this month's purchase count and so breaks for a shopper who has bought before but not this month.

I'm settling the went-well items for the lessons section: the Investigator Agent formed one candidate tying the failures to the flag change, the Mitigation Agent turned the flag back on as a reversible step rather than waiting for a code fix, and the revert was judged confirmed once the service left the incident level. I'm also noting that the Code-Fix Agent's draft pull request is up for a person to review. I'm not adding a flag-change reason item, since the record doesn't support it.

action_items.item: Make changes to io-shop feature flags roll out to a small share of requests first, and halt and revert them automatically when the error rate rises.
Add a CI test that renders io-shop account pages with each feature flag both on and off, using a shopper with past purchases but none this month.
Require that the flag-state account page test passes before a flag on io-shop can be changed in production.
Link the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop to an on-call rotation so that a person is paged when it fires.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' account page requests failed. The service's share of requests answered with server errors rose, and the service logged failed account page requests and warnings about the account page error rate.
Those account page requests raised ZeroDivisionError in the spend summary code in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py, and the account page turned each error into a failed page.

ruled_out.what: A code or config deploy: the production change events for the day before the onset held only this flag toggle, and no deploys came back.
Some other flag change: the flag provider's history held a single change by anyone but Argus in the hour it read, and that change is this toggle.
Shoppers closing the connection: those errors were already logged before the onset, at a time when the flag was on and account pages rendered normally.

causal_chain.step: At {P1.1} admin switched the feature flag legacy-checkout-fallback off. In the onset minute some account page requests already read the flag as off, every minute after that all of them did, and the ZeroDivisionError failures start in that same onset minute.

With the flag off, more account page requests went through render_spend_summary's monthly spend path, where average_spend_per_item_this_month divides by the number of this month's purchases, so it fails for a shopper who has bought before but not this month.

input.cause_in_plain_words: Switching off a feature setting sent more shoppers' account pages through a spending calculation that likely breaks for anyone who has bought nothing this month, because it divides by the number of this month's purchases.

contributing_factors.factor: No test was seen that covered average_spend_per_item_this_month, or render_spend_summary's monthly path, for a shopper with past purchases but none this month. The test file itself calls that the ordinary case.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A test with that shopper would have hit the division by zero, so the fault could have been fixed before the flag change exposed it to shoppers.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: The production change to legacy-checkout-fallback went from a share of requests to all of them almost at once. No staged rollout and no automatic halt on rising errors were seen.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The failures would have stayed within a small slice of requests, and the change would have been halted before it reached every shopper.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: No check was seen that exercised account pages with legacy-checkout-fallback off before it was switched off in production.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Account pages would have been seen failing with the flag off before the change was made to production.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent formed a single candidate, C1, that tied the failures to the flag change, after reading the metrics, the change events and the logs.
The Mitigation Agent turned legacy-checkout-fallback back on. That change can be put back and needs no code fix.
The Mitigation Agent judged the revert confirmed once it saw the service was no longer at the incident's level.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix with tests as a draft pull request for a person to review.

went_wrong: Nobody was paged: the alert was not linked to any on-call incident, so no person was called in to respond.

input.root_cause: `average_spend_per_item_this_month` in `src/io_shop/spend_summary.py` divides the account's spend this month by the number of purchases marked `in_current_month`, and it does not handle the case where that list is empty, which is the ordinary case for a shopper who has bought before but not this month. With legacy-checkout-fallback off, more account page requests went through `render_spend_summary`'s monthly path into this division, raised ZeroDivisionError, and `serve_account_page` turned each one into a failed page.
input.still_at_risk: Account page requests that still reach the monthly spend summary could fail for shoppers with no purchases this month, and switching legacy-checkout-fallback off again would bring the same failures back.
input.symptom: Shoppers' account pages failed to load
